IN A RECENT interview, James Dahle, creator of the popular White Coat Investor blog, talked about a change he’d made to his own personal portfolio: He described how he’d switched from purchasing individual bonds to opting instead for a bond fund.
Why the change? On the one hand, Dahle said, a ladder of individual bonds can be “a wonderful strategy.” But, he ultimately decided, purchasing bonds one by one felt like more trouble than it was worth. “It was too much of a pain.” So Dahle and his wife opted for the set-it-and-forget-it simplicity of a bond fund.
In discussing the motivation for this change, Dahle drew a distinction between two types of investors: “optimizers” and “satisficers.” Optimizers, as the term suggests, are folks who prefer to analyze decisions in as quantitative a way as possible.
What about satisficers? The term satisfice was coined in the 1950s by the economist Herbert A. Simon. His observation: In the face of limited information and limited time, most people seek to make decisions that are good enough and are willing to forgo the pursuit of more optimal results. Simon later won a Nobel Prize for this insight, and it’s an idea that’s broadly applicable to financial decisions.
As I’ve noted before, I believe there are two answers to every financial question: what the calculator says, and how you feel about it. Similarly, Dahle’s comments are a reminder that it can be okay to loosen the reins on financial decisions. As long as we’re choosing among reasonable options, we shouldn’t feel compelled to justify every decision quantitatively.
Below are three areas where you might employ the mindset of the satisficer.
Building a portfolio. People debate endlessly over portfolio strategy. Should you diversify internationally? Should you own a total-market fund or just the S&P 500? Should you tilt your portfolio toward value stocks? The list goes on. The problem in trying to answer these questions is that there’s data to support answers on both sides of each debate. That’s because, over time, investment strategies tend to go in and out of favor.
Consider the market’s recent performance. Year-to-date, value stocks are outperforming growth stocks by about 15 percentage points. But over the past ten years, it’s been a different story: Growth stocks have soundly beaten their value counterparts by more than 150 points cumulatively.
Patterns like this repeat all the time, with the result that it’s impossible to say definitively whether growth stocks or value stocks are necessarily “better.” It depends on the timeframe.
What does this mean in practice? On the one hand, it makes it difficult to ever reach a conclusive answer on nearly any investment question. But it also means that there’s little value in making frequent portfolio changes.
That’s why, when it comes to building a portfolio, I believe satisficing is the right answer. As long as you’ve chosen an investment strategy that’s reasonable enough, the most important thing, in my view, is to maintain the patience to stick with that strategy even when it’s out of favor. That’s because, if history is any guide, it will come back into favor at some point, and you want your portfolio to be there to benefit from that change when it arrives.
Managing a mortgage. If you’re among the fortunate homeowners with a mortgage rate in the 2% or 3% range, you may not have considered paying it down any faster than is required. That’s the rational decision, and in most cases, it will probably be what makes the most sense. Nonetheless, there can be reasons to pay off a mortgage even with an attractive rate.
If you’re heading into retirement, that’s when I’d give it serious consideration, and that’s because of the dynamics of household cash flow in retirement. Instead of adding to savings, retirees are withdrawing from their portfolios. That can make the state of the market much more of a day-to-day concern.
In theory, if a retiree has an appropriate asset allocation, then market volatility shouldn’t negatively impact their ability to meet expenses, including a mortgage, in retirement. But that’s just the theory. In practice, having low fixed costs can pay significant peace-of-mind dividends for folks in retirement when the market drops. That’s why I recommend going into retirement mortgage-free. It’s a case where you might sacrifice a little bit of financial efficiency for a benefit which can’t necessarily be quantified.
Structuring an estate plan. The federal estate tax now stands at 40%, and many states have their own estate or inheritance taxes as well. As a result, for many high-net-worth folks, it’s an almost obvious decision to put estate tax strategies in place. Consider a family that is $1 million over the federal estate tax threshold. Their estate would pay $400,000 in taxes at death. With such a significant exposure, almost any amount of legal fees for tax strategies would seem to be justified. And that’s certainly the route many wealthy individuals go. But not all.
Despite the sizable potential tax bill, some families forgo any estate tax planning. Why? A key reason is that these strategies require financial acrobatics which can be cumbersome and costly. For example, irrevocable trusts, which are probably the most common estate tax strategy, require their own tax returns. And they require a trustee, and trustees often ask to be paid. For these reasons, some families take a pass on these strategies. They know they’ll end up paying more in tax, but for them, the optimal path is the one that makes their lives simpler, even if it doesn’t look optimal on paper.
Financial decision-making requires a balance. On the one hand, we can’t ignore the numbers. But on the other, we should never feel too tightly bound by what the calculator says.
Adam M. Grossman is the founder of Mayport, a fixed-fee wealth management firm. Sign up for Adam's Daily Ideas email, follow him on X @AdamMGrossman and check out his earlier articles.
